arXiv:2011.03660v2 [cs.PL] 10 Nov 2020

Cost-Aware Type Theory

Yue Niu Note: yuen@andrew.cmu.edu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Robert Harper Note: rwh@cs.cmu.edu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University
Abstract

Although computational complexity is a fundamental aspect of program behavior, it is often at odds with common type theoretic principles such as function extensionality, which identifies all functions with the same input-output behavior. We present a computational type theory called 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} that has a primitive notion of cost (the number of evaluation steps). We introduce a new dependent function type “funtime” whose semantics can be viewed as a cost-aware version of function extensionality. We prove a collection of lemmas for 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT}, including a novel introduction rule for the new funtime type. 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} can be simultaneously viewed as a framework for analyzing computational complexity of programs and as the beginnings of a semantic foundation for characterizing feasible mathematical proofs.

1 Introduction

Beginning with mechanized time complexity analysis of Lisp programs [68], computational complexity in the context of programming language research has been studied from various perspectives, including definability of complexity classes inside type theory [21][22], syntactic characterizations of complexity classes [7][41][40], recurrence extraction [9][48], substructural & resource aware type systems [42][45][36], and program logics for interactive verification of cost bounds [19][54][32].

What seemed to be missing from the discussion was a semantic theory with a rich specification language in which computational complexity is a primitive notion. This is the main motivation behind the work in this article. The shift in perspective is subtle: instead of analyzing programs after the fact, we develop a theory for simultaneous construction of cost-aware specification and programs satisfying those specifications. This perspective on computational complexity resonates with a distinctive feature in dependent type theory: specifications are programs, and the construction of one is inextricably intertwined with the other.

We develop a computational dependent type theory, called 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} (cost-aware type theory), for analyzing the time complexity of programs. The central move borrows from the Martin-Löf ethos in the formulation of computational type theories: type structure internalizes prior judgmental notions. Following this idea, we introduce new judgment forms to describe computational complexity. A new dependent function type “funtime” is introduced to internalize the meaning of open judgments. We prove a novel introduction rule for the funtime type. The proof relies on the fact that a terminating recursive function induces a well-founded ordering on the recursive calls (a similar idea was introduced in [57] to add general recursion to Martin-Löf type theories).

A perhaps surprising fact is that the judgments in 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} only speak about total terms: there is no judgment form that acknowledges partiality. However, this is not achieved through syntactic means (such as Gödel’s T or system F). While syntactic restrictions alleviate the burden of the termination proof from the user, total languages are susceptible to arbitrary blow up in code size when compared to languages with general recursion [14].11 1 An article by Robert Harper discusses this in detail: https://existentialtype.wordpress.com/2014/03/20/old-neglected-theorems-are-still-theorems/.

Practically, programs in total languages can also have unexpected computational complexity. For example, a more liberal form of recursion can be simulated in Gödel’s T by proving course-of-value (COV) recursion (the dependently typed version is strong induction). One can then program via the COV-recursion interface, but the resulting algorithm will not have the expected recursive behavior: every recursive argument is considered, regardless of whether it was requested by the algorithm. This seems to be a fundamental limitation of programming with primitive recursion. Hence, while programs in Gödel’s T can be written in a more natural manner using an interface such as COV-recursion, their computational behavior and as a result complexity does not coincide with textbook algorithm analysis.

The key innovation in 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} leverages the synergetic relation between general recursion and cost specification: general recursion is needed to write algorithms with the expected cost, and the cost specification in turn enables one to prove that a general recursive function is total (and satisfies its functional specification). This enables the programmer to write general recursive functions that are not a priori terminating and simultaneously construct the proof that it is in fact terminating using the cost specification. As a consequence, the membership judgment M∈AM\in A immediately implies MM terminates, and all well-typed functions are total (an immediate consequence of adhering to a cost specification).

Language vs. machine Before diving into the specifics of 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT}, we take a moment to frame our work in the bigger landscape. While the programming languages theory encompasses nearly all imaginable computational behavior – e.g., state, randomization, parallelism, concurrency – language-based semantics for computational complexity has received comparatively little attention. Instead, machine models such as the Turing machine and RAM are incumbent in algorithmic complexity literature. Part of the reason for this discrepancy could be attributed to the belief that machine models are “lower-level” and so the induced computational complexity is a more accurate description of program performance in real life.

However, it should be noted that computational complexity defined in a language-based model (such as 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT}) do reflect real-life performance, as long as the implementation is resource bounded [12][31][13][11][61] by the cost semantics. This means that each stage of compilation (from the source language to the target language) is cost-preserving: the cost semantics of the higher-level language induces an upper bound on the cost semantics of the lower-level language. This process separates the concern of the algorithm analysis from low-level, implementation specific concerns that are asymptotically irrelevant in any case.

Furthermore, language-based models have some clear advantages compared to machine-models such as compositionality and modularity. Hence, a possible direction for future work would be designing intermediate languages for complexity analysis and the associated cost-preserving compilations, which would lead to a comprehensive framework for describing both high-level and low-level computational complexity and the effects of different compilation/scheduling strategies.

Outline In the following sections, we motivate and develop 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} and demonstrate the applicability of the theory with examples. In section 2, we set the stage by defining the underlying programming language 𝐏𝐋\mathbf{PL} and discuss some considerations when choosing an appropriate language for analyzing computational complexity. In section 3, we give some intuition for 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} by extending Martin-Löf’s meaning explanation for type theories to account for computational complexity. In section 4, we realize 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} via Allen’s PER-semantics [3] for computational type theories, which involves constructing a relation τ:𝒫⁡(𝖵𝖺𝗅×𝖵𝖺𝗅×𝒫⁡(𝖵𝖺𝗅×𝖵𝖺𝗅))\tau:\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{Val}\times\mathsf{Val}\times\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{Val}\times\mathsf{Val})) satisfying some coherence conditions. A coherent relation τ\tau is then a type system (in a technical sense), and the judgments of 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} are defined relative to a given type system τ\tau. In section 5, we define the judgments of 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} and prove some expected lemmas, including head expansion and the structural rules of hypothesis, weakening, and substitution. In section 6, we prove a collection of lemmas about the semantics of 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} constituting a simple proof theory that we later use to verify some example programs. In section 7, we discuss the usual assumptions made in algorithmic complexity and how they can be dealt with inside type theory. In section 8, we analyze the time complexity of Euclid’s algorithm for computing the greatest common divisor. In section 9 and 10, we extend 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} to account for parallelism and illustrate the extension by verifying the parallel complexity of computing the Fibonacci numbers. In section 11 and 12, we discuss some related work and promising directions for investigation.

2 Programming language for complexity analysis

Although there are various abstract notions of computational complexity, we focus on analyzing a simple and concrete cost measure – the number of steps a closed program takes to evaluate to a value. Under this view of complexity, the analysis is fundamentally about the specification and verification of behavioral properties of programs. Hence, the very nature of computational complexity suggests itself as an object of study inside computational type theories, in which typehood and membership are semantic properties, i.e., given by how programs compute. In the influential paper Constructive Mathematics and Computer Programming [53], Martin-Löf introduced a computational semantics for programming languages through what is known as the “meaning explanation”, a notion closely related to Tait’s method of logical relations [62] and Girard’s method of candidates of reducibility [30]. For dependent type theory, the same perspectives can also be found in the computational type theory of NuPRL [2], a program/proof refinement framework which has been used to verify a substantial amount of mathematics.

Programming language 𝐏𝐋\mathbf{PL} Following these computational type-theoretic approaches, we develop a dependent type theory called 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} (complexity-aware type theory) for analyzing computational complexity of programs. We begin by defining a programming language 𝐏𝐋\mathbf{PL} and an evaluation relation. The syntax of 𝐏𝐋\mathbf{PL} is given in Figure 1. Note that since typehood is a semantic property, there is no syntactic distinction between types and elements of a type. The value relation _​𝗏𝖺𝗅:𝒫⁡(𝖤𝗑𝗉)\_\;\mathsf{val}:\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{Exp}) and step relation _↦_:𝒫⁡(𝖤𝗑𝗉×𝖤𝗑𝗉)\_\mapsto\_:\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{Exp}\times\mathsf{Exp}) are defined in Figure 2. Write 𝖵𝖺𝗅={E∣E​𝗏𝖺𝗅}\mathsf{Val}=\{E\mid E\;\mathsf{val}\} for the set of closed programs that are values. Define evaluation as follows:

  1. 1.

    M⇓cVM\Downarrow^{c}V when M↦cVM\mapsto^{c}V and V​𝗏𝖺𝗅V\;\mathsf{val}.

  2. 2.

    M⇓VM\Downarrow V when there is a cc s.t. M⇓cVM\Downarrow^{c}V.

Where M↦cVM\mapsto^{c}V means MM transition to VV in exactly cc steps.

Complexity-aware function types In anticipation of analyzing complexity properties of programs, we introduce the new funtime type a:A→B⁡[P]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{a{:}A\to B}}{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{[P]}}, which classify functions that comply with the cost bound stated by PP. Crucially, PP is an open term of 𝐏𝐋\mathbf{PL} and not a natural number since the cost PP varies in the input value. Furthermore, it is also not a meta-theoretical function, because the variable aa ranges over terms of 𝐏𝐋\mathbf{PL}. This means we cannot directly use the ambient arithmetic functions in defining the cost component PP. One route would be to define all the usual arithmetic functions internally. This turns out to burden the mechanization process with many secondary proof obligations which hold in the ambient mathematics. Instead, we import a part of the ambient arithmetic world as foreign functions.

Foreign functions We introduce several syntactic operators that mediate the use of meta-theoretical functions or relations on natural numbers. The expression E1r^E2E_{1}\mathrel{\widehat{r}}E_{2} reifies a (meta-)relation r:ℕ×ℕr:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N} into a type, and f1^⁡(E)\mathop{\hat{f_{1}}}(E) and (E1f2^E2)(E_{1}\mathbin{\widehat{f_{2}}}E_{2}) form applications of (meta-)functions f1:ℕ→ℕf_{1}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} and f2:ℕ→ℕ→ℕf_{2}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}, respectively. In principle, we can define these constructs internally. However, we found it more practical to import these arithmetical facts and use them directly in the verification.

Evaluation strategy Usually, computational type theories are agnostic to the evaluation strategy employed by the programming language, i.e., one can define a type theory with either call by value or call by name evaluation. However, when considering computational complexity, different evaluation strategies can lead to wildly different evaluation costs. Often, call by name evaluation is favored because fewer rules are needed to specify the transition relation. This poses a barrier for complexity analysis, since if arbitrary computations can be applied to a function, it becomes difficult to prove uniform or general complexity properties about the function. Therefore, we opt for call by value evaluation; as a result, variables only range over values (elements of 𝖵𝖺𝗅\mathsf{Val}) in open term of 𝐏𝐋\mathbf{PL}.

3 Meaning explanation

Given a programming language, the meaning explanation propounded by Martin-Löf [53] specifies the meaning of types and membership via the execution behavior of the underlying programs; we give a brief introduction here. At the outset, there is the notion of canonical types. A canonical type is defined by specifying its equal canonical elements. This specification of equality is dependent on the canonical type in question, but in general it must be an equivalence relation on all members. In its basic form, the meaning explanation consists of four judgments:

A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾M∈A\displaystyle A\;\mathsf{type}\qquad M\in A
A≐A′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾M≐M′∈A\displaystyle A\doteq A^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}\qquad M\doteq M^{\prime}\in A

The first states that AA evaluates to a value A0A_{0}, and that A0A_{0} is a canonical type. Given that it is known that AA is a type (so that AA is known to evaluate to a canonical type A0A_{0}), the second states that MM evaluates to M0M_{0} and M0M_{0} is a canonical element of A0A_{0}. The third states that AA and A′A^{\prime} evaluates to equal canonical types. Lastly, given that AA is a type, the fourth states that MM and M′M^{\prime} evaluates to equal canonical members of the canonical type that AA evaluates to.

Following the philosophy that type constructors merely internalize prior judgmental structure, we add two new judgment forms, M∈A⁡[P]M\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}} and M≐M′∈A⁡[P]M\doteq M^{\prime}\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}} , which can be read as “MM in AA with cost PP” and “MM equal to M′M^{\prime} in AA with cost PP”. The first states that, presupposing AA is a type and PP is in 𝚗𝚊𝚝\mathtt{nat}(by the way we specify 𝚗𝚊𝚝\mathtt{nat}, this will mean PP evaluates to a numeral p¯\bar{p}), MM evaluates to M0M_{0} in cc steps, M0M_{0} is in AA, and that p≥cp\geq c. Similarly, the second states that (with the same presuppositions) MM evaluates to M0M_{0} in cc steps, M′M^{\prime} evaluates to M0′M^{\prime}_{0} in dd steps, M0M_{0} and M0′M^{\prime}_{0} are equal in AA, and that p≥max⁡(c,d)p\geq\max{(c,d)}. These two judgments express the meaning of the previous membership and equality judgments and in addition prescribe the evaluation costs of the subjects. Here, the evaluation costs of AA and PP are not mentioned, since we are analyzing the computational complexity of running code and not its specifications.22 2 If one desires, it is also possible to analyze the complexity of types by shifting the perspective and viewing them as elements of a universe.

Note that a careful staging of definitions is needed to specify the cost-bounded judgmental forms. Prior to even stating M∈A⁡[P]M\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}}, we need to know that PP is in 𝚗𝚊𝚝\mathtt{nat}, and hence that 𝚗𝚊𝚝\mathtt{nat} is a type. This also means it is not possible to define the judgment M∈AM\in A in terms of M∈A⁡[P]M\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}} by existentially quantifying PP, which would lead to an infinite regress of presuppositions.

4 Constructing a type system

The procedure given in the previous section of defining equal types and type membership is an instance of definition by induction-recursion, i.e., defining a structure inductively while simultaneously defining a function out of that structure. However, for mechanization purposes, it is more practical to follow the approach given by Allen [3] and define the judgments of type theory relative to a type system. Structurally, a type system is a relation τ:𝒫⁡(𝖵𝖺𝗅×𝖵𝖺𝗅×𝒫⁡(𝖵𝖺𝗅×𝖵𝖺𝗅))\tau:\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{Val}\times\mathsf{Val}\times\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{Val}\times\mathsf{Val})). The idea is that AA and BB are equal types with membership relation ϕ\phi exactly when τ⁡(A,B,ϕ)\tau(A,B,\phi). Observe that in the meaning explanation, 1) type equality and membership are partial equivalence relations, and 2) equal types classify the same terms. Hence, τ\tau must satisfy the same coherence properties in order to qualify as a type system, which can be summarized as follows.

Definition 4.1 (Type Systems).

Write 𝖯𝖳𝖲=𝒫⁡(𝖵𝖺𝗅×𝖵𝖺𝗅×𝒫⁡(𝖵𝖺𝗅×𝖵𝖺𝗅))\mathsf{PTS}=\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{Val}\times\mathsf{Val}\times\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{Val}\times\mathsf{Val})) for the space of all possible type systems. Let τ:𝖯𝖳𝖲\tau:\mathsf{PTS}. τ\tau is a type system when the following conditions hold:

  1. 1.

    Unicity: τ⁡(A,B,ϕ)\tau(A,B,\phi) and τ⁡(A,B,ϕ′)\tau(A,B,\phi^{\prime}) implies ϕ=ϕ′\phi=\phi^{\prime}.

  2. 2.

    PER valuation: τ⁡(A,B,ϕ)\tau(A,B,\phi) implies ϕ\phi is a PER.

  3. 3.

    Symmetry: τ⁡(A,B,ϕ)\tau(A,B,\phi) implies τ⁡(B,A,ϕ)\tau(B,A,\phi).

  4. 4.

    Transitivity: τ⁡(A,B,ϕ)\tau(A,B,\phi) and τ⁡(B,C,ϕ)\tau(B,C,\phi) implies τ⁡(A,C,ϕ)\tau(A,C,\phi).

Now, to define a possible type system τ\tau closed under type constructors and to show that it is a type system, we follow the construction presented by Angiuli [4] and define two hierarchies of possible type systems τn\tau_{n} and vnv_{n}, the latter of which forms a cumulative universe hierarchy. Roughly, each τn\tau_{n} contains all types from the previous level and the universes in vnv_{n} and closes them under the type constructors, and vnv_{n} contains all universes 𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i\mathtt{Univ}_{i} with i<ni<n. Since M1⇓c+1VM_{1}\Downarrow^{c+1}V and M2⇓c′+1V′M_{2}\Downarrow^{c^{\prime}+1}V^{\prime}, it suffices to show p+1≥max⁡(c+1,c′+1)p+1\geq\max(c+1,c^{\prime}+1), which holds.

Theorem 4.2 (Monotonicity).
  1. 1.

    For all v:𝖯𝖳𝖲v:\mathsf{PTS}, Types​(v,_)\text{Types}(v,\_) is monotone.

  2. 2.

    For all τ:𝖯𝖳𝖲\tau:\mathsf{PTS}, Types​(_,τ)\text{Types}(\_,\tau) is monotone.

Proof.

By case analysis on each clause of Types. ∎

Lemma 4.3 (Closure under Types).

If v:𝖯𝖳𝖲v:\mathsf{PTS} is a type system, then μ​τ.Types​(v,τ)\mu\tau.\,\text{Types}(v,\tau) is also a type system.

Proof.

By case analysis on each clause of Types. ∎

Lemma 4.4 (Empty type system).

∅:𝖯𝖳𝖲\emptyset:\mathsf{PTS} is a type system.

Proof.

The criteria for type system hold vacuously. ∎

Lemma 4.5.

τ0\tau_{0} is a type system.

Proof.

By Lemma 4.4 and 4.3. ∎

Theorem 4.6 (Hierarchy).

For all n:ℕn:\mathbb{N}, vnv_{n} and τn\tau_{n} are type systems.

Proof.

By strong induction on nn, using Lemma 4.4 and 4.5 in the base case and Lemma 4.3 in the inductive case. ∎

Theorem 4.7.

vωv_{\omega} is a type system.

Proof.

Unicity, symmetry, and transitivity are immediate; per valuation follows from Lemma 4.6. ∎

Theorem 4.8.

τω\tau_{\omega} is a type system.

Proof.

By Lemma 4.7 and 4.3. ∎

Lemma 4.9.

Let XX be a complete lattice and f,g:X→Xf,g:X\to X be monotone functions. If f⁡(x)⊆g⁡(x)f(x)\subseteq g(x) for all x∈Xx\in X, then μ​x.f⁡(x)⊆μ​x.g⁡(x)\mu x.\,f(x)\subseteq\mu x.\,g(x).

Proof.

μ​x.g⁡(x)\mu x.\,g(x) is ff-closed because f(μx.g(x))⊆g(μx.g(x))=μx.g(x)f(\mu x.\,g(x))\subseteq g(\mu x.\,g(x))=\mu x.\,g(x). Since μ​x.f⁡(x)\mu x.\,f(x) is the least ff-closed point, μ​x.f⁡(x)⊆μ​x.g⁡(x)\mu x.\,f(x)\subseteq\mu x.\,g(x). ∎

Lemma 4.10 (Cumulativity).
  1. 1.

    vi⊆vωv_{i}\subseteq v_{\omega} for all ii.

  2. 2.

    τi⊆τω\tau_{i}\subseteq\tau_{\omega} for all ii.

Proof.

The first part holds by construction. For the latter, by Lemma 4.9, it suffices to show Types​(vi,τ)⊆Types​(vω,τ)\text{Types}(v_{i},\tau)\subseteq\text{Types}(v_{\omega},\tau) for all τ\tau. It suffices to show Types​(_,τ)\text{Types}(\_,\tau) is monotone, which holds by Lemma 4.2. ∎

5 Computational Type Theory

Closed Judgments Having defined a type system τω\tau_{\omega}, we are now in a position to define the judgments of 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT}. In addition to the usual type equality and membership relation, we define a third membership relation which bounds the evaluation cost.

Definition 5.1 (Types and Equality).

Given a type system τ\tau,

  1. 1.

    A≐B​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾A\doteq B\;\mathsf{type} when A∼B↓α∈τA\sim B\downarrow\alpha\in\tau for some α\alpha.

    M≐M′∈A⁡[P]M\doteq M^{\prime}\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}} when A∼A↓α∈τA\sim A\downarrow\alpha\in\tau and M∼M′∈α⁡[P]M\sim M^{\prime}\in\alpha\;{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{[P]}} for some α\alpha.

  4. 4.

    A≐B​𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾A\doteq B\;\mathsf{true} when A∼B↓α∈τA\sim B\downarrow\alpha\in\tau and M∼M∈αM\sim M\in\alpha for some α\alpha and MM.

Remark.

This definition is generic in a type system τ\tau. However, from now on we will implicitly assume τ=τω\tau=\tau_{\omega} unless specified otherwise.

The reflexive case for the 3 relations will be abbreviated as follows:

  1. 1.

    A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾A\;\mathsf{type} means A≐A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾A\doteq A\;\mathsf{type}.

  2. 2.

    M∈AM\in A means M≐M∈AM\doteq M\in A.

  3. 3.

    M∈A⁡[P]M\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}} means M≐M∈A⁡[P]M\doteq M\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}} .

Furthermore, when an expression is a value, membership will be subscripted with a 0: M≐M′∈0AM\doteq M^{\prime}\in_{0}A when M​𝗏𝖺𝗅M\;\mathsf{val}, M′​𝗏𝖺𝗅M^{\prime}\;\mathsf{val}, and M≐M′∈AM\doteq M^{\prime}\in A, and M∈0AM\in_{0}A when M​𝗏𝖺𝗅M\;\mathsf{val} and M∈AM\in A.

Lemma 5.1 (Closed PER).

Lemma 5.2.

Given A≐A′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾A\doteq A^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type},

  1. 1.

Proof.

  1. 1.

    By assumption, A∼A′↓α∈τωA\sim A^{\prime}\downarrow\alpha\in\tau_{\omega} for some α\alpha. By assumption, M⇓VM\Downarrow V, M′⇓V′M^{\prime}\Downarrow V^{\prime}, and α⁡(V,V′)\alpha(V,V^{\prime}). Hence M′′⇓VM^{\prime\prime}\Downarrow V, and we are done.

Hence we have M′′⇓c+1VM^{\prime\prime}\Downarrow^{c+1}V and 𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(P)⇓p+1¯{\mathtt{suc}}(P)\Downarrow\bar{p+1}. It suffices to show p+1≥max⁡(c+1,c′)p+1\geq\max{(c+1,c^{\prime})}, which holds.

Open Judgments To extend the closed judgments to open terms, we define Γ​𝗍𝖾𝗅𝖾\Gamma\;\mathsf{tele}, which represent telescopes.

Open judgments are given meaning by functionality: open types are equal if all equal substitution instances are equal as closed types, and similarly for membership. As before, substitution instances range over values.

Given Γ​𝗍𝖾𝗅𝖾\Gamma\;\mathsf{tele}, define γ∼γ′∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma:

  3. 3.

Γ≫V≐V′∈0A\Gamma\gg V\doteq V^{\prime}\in_{0}A ⇔\iff Γ≫V≐V′∈A⁡[𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘]\Gamma\gg V\doteq V^{\prime}\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[{\mathtt{zero}}]}}.

In order to prove some structural lemmas about the open judgments (such as symmetry and transitivity), we need to restrict Γ\Gamma to telescopes that are also contexts:

Definition 5.5 (Contexts).

Given Γ​𝗍𝖾𝗅𝖾\Gamma\;\mathsf{tele}, and Γ′​𝗍𝖾𝗅𝖾\Gamma^{\prime}\;\mathsf{tele}, define Γ≐Γ′​𝖼𝗍𝗑\Gamma\doteq\Gamma^{\prime}\;\mathsf{ctx}:

  2. 2.

Lemma 5.5 (PER of contexts).

Given Γ≐Γ​𝖼𝗍𝗑\Gamma\doteq\Gamma\;\mathsf{ctx},

  1. 1.

    If γ1∼γ2∈Γ\gamma_{1}\sim\gamma_{2}\in\Gamma, then γ2∼γ1∈Γ\gamma_{2}\sim\gamma_{1}\in\Gamma.

Proof.

Part 1): induction on the length of Γ\Gamma. If Γ=⋅\Gamma=\cdot, then the result follows by definition. Otherwise, Γ=Γ′,a:A\Gamma=\Gamma^{\prime},a{:}A, and suppose γ1,[a↦V1]∼γ2,[a↦V2]∈Γ′,a:A\gamma_{1},[a\mapsto V_{1}]\sim\gamma_{2},[a\mapsto V_{2}]\in\Gamma^{\prime},a{:}A. We need to show γ2,[a↦V2]∼γ1,[a↦V1]∈Γ′,a:A\gamma_{2},[a\mapsto V_{2}]\sim\gamma_{1},[a\mapsto V_{1}]\in\Gamma^{\prime},a{:}A. By definition, it suffices to show

  1. 1.

    V2≐V1∈0γ^2AV_{2}\doteq V_{1}\in_{0}\hat{\gamma}_{2}A

  2. 2.

    γ2∼γ1∈Γ′\gamma_{2}\sim\gamma_{1}\in\Gamma^{\prime}

By the assumption that Γ≐Γ​𝖼𝗍𝗑\Gamma\doteq\Gamma\;\mathsf{ctx}, we have Γ′≫A≐A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma^{\prime}\gg A\doteq A\;\mathsf{type} and Γ′≐Γ′​𝖼𝗍𝗑\Gamma^{\prime}\doteq\Gamma^{\prime}\;\mathsf{ctx}. By assumption, we have V1≐V2∈0γ^1AV_{1}\doteq V_{2}\in_{0}\hat{\gamma}_{1}A and γ1∼γ2∈Γ′\gamma_{1}\sim\gamma_{2}\in\Gamma^{\prime}. Hence the second obligation follows by induction. The first obligation follows from Lemma 5.1 and 5.2, given that we show γ^1​A≐γ^2​A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}_{1}A\doteq\hat{\gamma}_{2}A\;\mathsf{type}, which in turn follows by definition of Γ′≫A≐A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma^{\prime}\gg A\doteq A\;\mathsf{type}.

Part 2): induction on the length of Γ\Gamma. If Γ=⋅\Gamma=\cdot, then the result is immediate. Otherwise, Γ=Γ′,a:A\Gamma=\Gamma^{\prime},a{:}A. Suppose γ1,[a↦V1]∼γ2,[a↦V2]∈Γ′,a:A\gamma_{1},[a\mapsto V_{1}]\sim\gamma_{2},[a\mapsto V_{2}]\in\Gamma^{\prime},a{:}A and γ2,[a↦V2]∼γ3,[a↦V3]∈Γ′,a:A\gamma_{2},[a\mapsto V_{2}]\sim\gamma_{3},[a\mapsto V_{3}]\in\Gamma^{\prime},a{:}A. We need to show γ1,[a↦V1]∼γ3,[a↦V3]∈Γ′,a:A\gamma_{1},[a\mapsto V_{1}]\sim\gamma_{3},[a\mapsto V_{3}]\in\Gamma^{\prime},a{:}A. By definition, it suffices to show

  1. 1.

    V1≐V3∈0γ^1AV_{1}\doteq V_{3}\in_{0}\hat{\gamma}_{1}A

  2. 2.

    γ1∼γ3∈Γ′\gamma_{1}\sim\gamma_{3}\in\Gamma^{\prime}

By the assumptions, we have

  1. 1.

    Γ′≐Γ′​𝖼𝗍𝗑\Gamma^{\prime}\doteq\Gamma^{\prime}\;\mathsf{ctx}

  2. 2.

    Γ′≫A≐A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma^{\prime}\gg A\doteq A\;\mathsf{type}

  3. 3.

    V1≐V2∈0γ^1AV_{1}\doteq V_{2}\in_{0}\hat{\gamma}_{1}A

  4. 4.

    γ1∼γ2∈Γ′\gamma_{1}\sim\gamma_{2}\in\Gamma^{\prime}

  5. 5.

Hence we have γ^1​A≐γ^2​A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}_{1}A\doteq\hat{\gamma}_{2}A\;\mathsf{type}. By Lemma 5.2, this implies V2≐V3∈0γ^1AV_{2}\doteq V_{3}\in_{0}\hat{\gamma}_{1}A, and by Lemma 5.1 we get V1≐V3∈0γ^1AV_{1}\doteq V_{3}\in_{0}\hat{\gamma}_{1}A. Lemma 5.6 (PER of open judgments).

Given Γ≐Γ​𝖼𝗍𝗑\Gamma\doteq\Gamma\;\mathsf{ctx},

  1. 1.

    Γ≫_≐_​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg\_\doteq\_\;\mathsf{type} is a PER.

  2. 2.

    If Γ≫A≐A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg A\doteq A\;\mathsf{type}, then Γ≫_≐_∈A\Gamma\gg\_\doteq\_\in A is a PER.

  3. 3.

    If Γ≫A≐A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg A\doteq A\;\mathsf{type} and Γ≫P≐P∈𝚗𝚊𝚝\Gamma\gg P\doteq P\in\mathtt{nat}, then Γ≫_≐_∈A⁡[P]\Gamma\gg\_\doteq\_\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}} is a PER.

Proof.

For part 1), suppose Γ≫A1≐A2​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg A_{1}\doteq A_{2}\;\mathsf{type}. We need to show Γ≫A2≐A1​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg A_{2}\doteq A_{1}\;\mathsf{type}. Let γ∼γ′∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma. It suffices to show γ^​A2≐γ^′​A1​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}A_{2}\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}A_{1}\;\mathsf{type}. By Lemma 5.5, γ′∼γ∈Γ\gamma^{\prime}\sim\gamma\in\Gamma, so by assumption, γ^′​A1≐γ^​A2​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}A_{1}\doteq\hat{\gamma}A_{2}\;\mathsf{type}. Hence the result follows by Lemma 5.1.

Now suppose Γ≫A1≐A2​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg A_{1}\doteq A_{2}\;\mathsf{type} and Γ≫A2≐A3​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg A_{2}\doteq A_{3}\;\mathsf{type}. We need to show Γ≫A1≐A3​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg A_{1}\doteq A_{3}\;\mathsf{type}. Let γ∼γ′∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma. It suffices to show γ^​A1≐γ^′​A3​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}A_{1}\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}A_{3}\;\mathsf{type}. By Lemma 5.5, γ∼γ∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma\in\Gamma, so by assumption, γ^​A1≐γ^​A2​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}A_{1}\doteq\hat{\gamma}A_{2}\;\mathsf{type} and γ^​A2≐γ^′​A3​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}A_{2}\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}A_{3}\;\mathsf{type}. Hence the result follows by Lemma 5.1. Part 2) - 3) follow similarly. ∎

Head expansion can be extended to open judgments. Write Γ≫E↦E′\Gamma\gg E\mapsto E^{\prime} if for all γ∼γ∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma\in\Gamma, γ^E↦∗γ^E′\hat{\gamma}E\mapsto^{*}\hat{\gamma}E^{\prime}.

Lemma 5.7 (Open head expansion).

Given Γ≐Γ​𝖼𝗍𝗑\Gamma\doteq\Gamma\;\mathsf{ctx},

  1. 1.

    If Γ≫A≐A′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg A\doteq A^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type} and Γ≫A′′↦A\Gamma\gg A^{\prime\prime}\mapsto A, then Γ≫A′′≐A′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg A^{\prime\prime}\doteq A^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}.

  2. 2.

    If Γ≫M≐M′∈A\Gamma\gg M\doteq M^{\prime}\in A and Γ≫M′′↦M\Gamma\gg M^{\prime\prime}\mapsto M, then Γ≫M′′≐M′∈A\Gamma\gg M^{\prime\prime}\doteq M^{\prime}\in A.

Proof.

  1. 1.

    Let γ∼γ′∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma. We need to show γ^​A′′≐γ^′​A′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}A^{\prime\prime}\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}A^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}. By assumption, we know γ^​A≐γ^′​A′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}A\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}A^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}. Since Γ≐Γ​𝖼𝗍𝗑\Gamma\doteq\Gamma\;\mathsf{ctx}, γ∼γ∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma\in\Gamma, so we have γ^A′′↦∗γ^A\hat{\gamma}A^{\prime\prime}\mapsto^{*}\hat{\gamma}A, so the result follows from Lemma 5.3.

  2. 2.

    Let γ∼γ′∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma. We need to show γ^​M′′≐γ^′​M′∈γ^​A\hat{\gamma}M^{\prime\prime}\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}M^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}A. By assumption, we know γ^​M≐γ^′​M′∈γ^​A\hat{\gamma}M\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}M^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}A. Since Γ≐Γ​𝖼𝗍𝗑\Gamma\doteq\Gamma\;\mathsf{ctx}, γ∼γ∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma\in\Gamma, so we have γ^M′′↦∗γ^M\hat{\gamma}M^{\prime\prime}\mapsto^{*}\hat{\gamma}M, so the result follows from Lemma 5.3.

∎

Open judgments admit the structural rules of identity, weakening, and substitution:

Lemma 5.8 (Hypothesis).

Γ,a:A≫a∈A⁡[𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘]\Gamma,a{:}A\gg a\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[{\mathtt{zero}}]}}.

Proof.

Let γ,[a↦V]∼γ′,[a↦V′]∈Γ,a:A\gamma,[a\mapsto V]\sim\gamma^{\prime},[a\mapsto V^{\prime}]\in\Gamma,a{:}A. We need to show V≐V′∈γ^​A​[𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘]V\doteq V^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[{\mathtt{zero}}]}} , which holds by definition of γ,[a↦V]∼γ′,[a↦V′]∈Γ,a:A\gamma,[a\mapsto V]\sim\gamma^{\prime},[a\mapsto V^{\prime}]\in\Gamma,a{:}A. ∎

Lemma 5.9 (Weakening).
  1. 1.

    If Γ≫B≐B′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg B\doteq B^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}, then Γ,a:A≫B≐B′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma,a{:}A\gg B\doteq B^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}.

  2. 2.

    If Γ≫M≐M′∈B\Gamma\gg M\doteq M^{\prime}\in B, then Γ,a:A≫M≐M′∈B\Gamma,a{:}A\gg M\doteq M^{\prime}\in B.

  3. 3.

    If Γ≫M≐M′∈B⁡[P]\Gamma\gg M\doteq M^{\prime}\in B{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}}, then Γ,a:A≫M≐M′∈B⁡[P]\Gamma,a{:}A\gg M\doteq M^{\prime}\in B{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}}.

Proof.

For part 1, let γ,[a↦V]∼γ′,[a↦V′]∈Γ,a:A\gamma,[a\mapsto V]\sim\gamma^{\prime},[a\mapsto V^{\prime}]\in\Gamma,a{:}A. We need to show γ^​B≐γ^​B′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}B\doteq\hat{\gamma}B^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}. By definition, γ∼γ′∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma, so the result follows from assumption. Part 2 and 3 follow similarly. ∎

For sequencing operations occurring in types and cost specifications, we write ⟨E1/a⟩​E2\left<E_{1}/a\right>E_{2} for 𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=E1​𝚒𝚗​E2\mathtt{let}\;a=E_{1}\;\mathtt{in}\;E_{2}.

Remark.

“leftist” substitution is required because untyped principles such as direct computation [43] does not hold in 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT}. In contrast to NuPRL, types can internalize cost-aware judgments, and so in general membership is not invariant under untyped rewrite rules.

Lemma 5.10 (Substitution).
  1. 1.

    If Γ≫M≐M′∈A\Gamma\gg M\doteq M^{\prime}\in A and Γ,a:A≫B≐B′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma,a{:}A\gg B\doteq B^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}, then Γ≫⟨M/a⟩​B≐⟨M′/a⟩​B′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\Gamma\gg\left<M/a\right>B\doteq\left<M^{\prime}/a\right>B^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}.

  2. 2.

    If Γ≫M≐M′∈A\Gamma\gg M\doteq M^{\prime}\in A and Γ,a:A≫N≐N′∈B\Gamma,a{:}A\gg N\doteq N^{\prime}\in B, then Γ≫𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=M​𝚒𝚗​N≐𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=M′​𝚒𝚗​N′∈⟨M/a⟩​B\Gamma\gg\mathtt{let}\;a=M\;\mathtt{in}\;N\doteq\mathtt{let}\;a=M^{\prime}\;\mathtt{in}\;N^{\prime}\in\left<M/a\right>B.

  3. 3.

    If Γ≫M≐M′∈A⁡[P]\Gamma\gg M\doteq M^{\prime}\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}} and Γ,a:A≫N≐N′∈B⁡[Q]\Gamma,a{:}A\gg N\doteq N^{\prime}\in B{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[Q]}}, then Γ≫𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=M​𝚒𝚗​N≐𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=M′​𝚒𝚗​N′∈⟨M/a⟩​B​[P​+^​𝚜𝚞𝚌​(⟨M/a⟩​Q)]\Gamma\gg\mathtt{let}\;a=M\;\mathtt{in}\;N\doteq\mathtt{let}\;a=M^{\prime}\;\mathtt{in}\;N^{\prime}\in\left<M/a\right>B{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P\hat{+}{\mathtt{suc}}(\left<M/a\right>Q)]}}.

Proof.

  1. 1.

    Let γ∼γ′∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma. We need to show γ^​⟨M/a⟩​B≐γ^′​⟨M′/a⟩​B′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}\left<M/a\right>B\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}\left<M^{\prime}/a\right>B^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}. By assumption, we have γ^​M≐γ^′​M′∈γ^​A\hat{\gamma}M\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}M^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}A. This means that

    1. (a)

      γ^​M⇓V\hat{\gamma}M\Downarrow V

    2. (b)

      γ^′​M′⇓V′\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}M^{\prime}\Downarrow V^{\prime}

    and V≐V′∈0γ^AV\doteq V^{\prime}\in_{0}\hat{\gamma}A. By definition, γ,[a↦V]∼γ′,[a↦V′]∈Γ,a:A\gamma,[a\mapsto V]\sim\gamma^{\prime},[a\mapsto V^{\prime}]\in\Gamma,a{:}A, so by assumption, γ^​[V/a]​B≐γ^​[V′/a]​B′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\hat{\gamma}[V/a]B\doteq\hat{\gamma}[V^{\prime}/a]B^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}, and the result follows from Lemma 5.3.

  2. 2.

    Let γ∼γ′∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma. We need to show γ^​𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=M​𝚒𝚗​N≐γ^′​𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=M′​𝚒𝚗​N′∈γ^​⟨M/a⟩​B\hat{\gamma}\mathtt{let}\;a=M\;\mathtt{in}\;N\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}\mathtt{let}\;a=M^{\prime}\;\mathtt{in}\;N^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}\left<M/a\right>B. By assumption, we have γ^​M≐γ^′​M′∈γ^​A\hat{\gamma}M\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}M^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}A. This means that

    1. (a)

      γ^​M⇓V\hat{\gamma}M\Downarrow V

    2. (b)

      γ^′​M′⇓V′\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}M^{\prime}\Downarrow V^{\prime}

    and V≐V′∈0γ^AV\doteq V^{\prime}\in_{0}\hat{\gamma}A. By definition, γ,[a↦V]∼γ′,[a↦V′]∈Γ,a:A\gamma,[a\mapsto V]\sim\gamma^{\prime},[a\mapsto V^{\prime}]\in\Gamma,a{:}A, so by assumption, γ^​[V/a]​N≐γ^′​[V′/a]​N′∈γ^​[V/a]​B\hat{\gamma}[V/a]N\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}[V^{\prime}/a]N^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}[V/a]B, and the result follows from Lemma 5.3.

  3. 3.

    Let γ∼γ′∈Γ\gamma\sim\gamma^{\prime}\in\Gamma. We need to show γ^​𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=M​𝚒𝚗​N≐γ^′​𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=M′​𝚒𝚗​N′∈γ^​⟨M/a⟩​B​[γ^​P​+^​𝚜𝚞𝚌​(⟨M/a⟩​Q)]\hat{\gamma}\mathtt{let}\;a=M\;\mathtt{in}\;N\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}\mathtt{let}\;a=M^{\prime}\;\mathtt{in}\;N^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}\left<M/a\right>B{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[\hat{\gamma}P\hat{+}{\mathtt{suc}}(\left<M/a\right>Q)]}} . By assumption, we have γ^​M≐γ^′​M′∈γ^​A​[γ^​P]\hat{\gamma}M\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}M^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[\hat{\gamma}P]}} . This means that

    1. (a)

      γ^M⇓cV\hat{\gamma}M\Downarrow^{c}V

    2. (b)

      γ^′M′⇓c′V′\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}M^{\prime}\Downarrow^{c^{\prime}}V^{\prime}

    3. (c)

      γ^​P⇓p¯\hat{\gamma}P\Downarrow\bar{p}

    4. (d)

      p≥max⁡(c,c′)p\geq\max(c,c^{\prime})

    Hence V≐V′∈0γ^AV\doteq V^{\prime}\in_{0}\hat{\gamma}A. By definition, γ,[a↦V]∼γ′,[a↦V′]∈Γ,a:A\gamma,[a\mapsto V]\sim\gamma^{\prime},[a\mapsto V^{\prime}]\in\Gamma,a{:}A, so by assumption, γ^​[V/a]​N≐γ^′​[V′/a]​N′∈γ^​[V/a]​B​[γ^​[V/a]​Q]\hat{\gamma}[V/a]N\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}[V^{\prime}/a]N^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}[V/a]B{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[\hat{\gamma}[V/a]Q]}} . By Lemma 5.3, we have γ^​[V/a]​N≐γ^′​[V′/a]​N′∈γ^​⟨M/a⟩​B​[γ^​⟨M/a⟩​Q]\hat{\gamma}[V/a]N\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}[V^{\prime}/a]N^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}\left<M/a\right>B{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[\hat{\gamma}\left<M/a\right>Q]}} . By Lemma 5.3, we have γ^​𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=M​𝚒𝚗​N≐γ^′​𝚕𝚎𝚝​a=M′​𝚒𝚗​N′∈γ^​⟨M/a⟩​B​[γ^​P​+^​𝚜𝚞𝚌​(γ^​⟨M/a⟩​Q)]\hat{\gamma}\mathtt{let}\;a=M\;\mathtt{in}\;N\doteq\hat{\gamma}^{\prime}\mathtt{let}\;a=M^{\prime}\;\mathtt{in}\;N^{\prime}\in\hat{\gamma}\left<M/a\right>B{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[\hat{\gamma}P\hat{+}{\mathtt{suc}}(\hat{\gamma}\left<M/a\right>Q)]}} , as required.

∎

Semantics of types Since type systems satisfy unicity, it is sometimes useful to refer to the denotation of types, i.e. the unique PER designated as its membership relation.

Lemma 5.11 (Closed denotation).

If A​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾A\;\mathsf{type}, then there is a unique α\alpha such that A∼A↓α∈τωA\sim A\downarrow\alpha\in\tau_{\omega}. Write this as α=⟦A⟧\alpha=\llbracket A\rrbracket.

Proof.

By unicity of τω\tau_{\omega}. ∎

Lemma 5.12 (Open denotation).

Given A∼A′↓α∈τiA\sim A^{\prime}\downarrow\alpha\in\tau_{i} and a:A≫B≐B′∈𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟ia{:}A\gg B\doteq B^{\prime}\in\mathtt{Univ}_{i}, there is a β\beta such that a:α​⊳​B∼B′↓β∈τia{:}\alpha\rhd B\sim B^{\prime}\downarrow\beta\in\tau_{i}. Write this as β=⟦a:α.(B,B′)⟧\beta=\llbracket a{:}\alpha.(B,B^{\prime})\rrbracket.

Proof.

First, we need to construct β\beta. Let V,V′V,V^{\prime} such that α⁡(V,V′)\alpha(V,V^{\prime}). By assumption, we have [V/a]​B≐[V′/a]​B′∈𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i[V/a]B\doteq[V^{\prime}/a]B^{\prime}\in\mathtt{Univ}_{i}. This means [V/a]​B∼[V′/a]​B′↓ϕ∈τi[V/a]B\sim[V^{\prime}/a]B^{\prime}\downarrow\phi\in\tau_{i} for some ϕ\phi. Let β=(V,V′)↦ϕ\beta=(V,V^{\prime})\mapsto\phi. We need to show a:α​⊳​B∼B′↓β∈τia{:}\alpha\rhd B\sim B^{\prime}\downarrow\beta\in\tau_{i}. Let V,V′V,V^{\prime} such that α⁡(V,V′)\alpha(V,V^{\prime}). It suffices to show [V/a]​B∼[V′/a]​B′↓βV,V′∈τi[V/a]B\sim[V^{\prime}/a]B^{\prime}\downarrow\beta_{V,V^{\prime}}\in\tau_{i}, which holds by definition of β\beta. ∎

Lemma 5.13 (Functionality).

If a:α​⊳​B∼B′↓β∈τωa{:}\alpha\rhd B\sim B^{\prime}\downarrow\beta\in\tau_{\omega}, then βV,V=βV,V′\beta_{V,V}=\beta_{V,V^{\prime}} for all α⁡(V,V)\alpha(V,V) and α⁡(V,V′)\alpha(V,V^{\prime}).

Proof.

Let V,V′V,V^{\prime} such that α⁡(V,V)\alpha(V,V) and α⁡(V,V′)\alpha(V,V^{\prime}). By assumption, we have

  1. 1.

    [V/a]​B∼[V/a]​B′↓βV,V∈τω[V/a]B\sim[V/a]B^{\prime}\downarrow\beta_{V,V}\in\tau_{\omega}

  2. 2.

    [V/a]​B∼[V′/a]​B′↓βV,V′∈τω[V/a]B\sim[V^{\prime}/a]B^{\prime}\downarrow\beta_{V,V^{\prime}}\in\tau_{\omega}

Apply symmetry and transitivity:

[V/a]​B′∼[V/a]​B↓βV,V∈τω\displaystyle[V/a]B^{\prime}\sim[V/a]B\downarrow\beta_{V,V}\in\tau_{\omega}
[V/a]​B∼[V/a]​B↓βV,V∈τω\displaystyle[V/a]B\sim[V/a]B\downarrow\beta_{V,V}\in\tau_{\omega} (5.1)
[V′/a]​B′∼[V/a]​B↓βV,V′∈τω\displaystyle[V^{\prime}/a]B^{\prime}\sim[V/a]B\downarrow\beta_{V,V^{\prime}}\in\tau_{\omega}
[V/a]​B∼[V/a]​B↓βV,V′∈τω\displaystyle[V/a]B\sim[V/a]B\downarrow\beta_{V,V^{\prime}}\in\tau_{\omega} (5.2)

Thus by unicity with (5.1) and (5.2) we have βV,V=βV,V′\beta_{V,V}=\beta_{V,V^{\prime}}. ∎

Lemma 5.14 (Open computation).

Given A∼A′↓α∈τωA\sim A^{\prime}\downarrow\alpha\in\tau_{\omega}, a:A≫B≐B​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾a{:}A\gg B\doteq B\;\mathsf{type}, and a:A≫N≐N′∈Ba{:}A\gg N\doteq N^{\prime}\in B, there is a β\beta such that a:α​⊳​B∼B′↓β∈τωa{:}\alpha\rhd B\sim B^{\prime}\downarrow\beta\in\tau_{\omega} and a:α​⊳​N∼N′∈βa{:}\alpha\rhd N\sim N^{\prime}\in\beta .

Proof.

The first part is the same as in Lemma 5.12. For the latter, let V,V′V,V^{\prime} such that α⁡(V,V′)\alpha(V,V^{\prime}). We need to show [V/a]​N∼[V′/a]​N′∈βV,V′[V/a]N\sim[V^{\prime}/a]N^{\prime}\in\beta_{V,V^{\prime}}. By assumption, [V/a]​N≐[V′/a]​N′∈[V/a]​B[V/a]N\doteq[V^{\prime}/a]N^{\prime}\in[V/a]B. So it suffices to show ⟦[V/a]​B⟧=βV,V′\llbracket[V/a]B\rrbracket=\beta_{V,V^{\prime}}, which follows from Lemma 5.13. ∎

6 Semantic Proof Theory

In the context of computational type theories, a proof theory could be viewed as a collection of generally useful lemmas about the semantic construction. As such, it is not the least set of derivable facts from the collection, and issues of admissibility of rules do not arise in this setting. This is a pragmatic approach, as it is often convenient to extend the proof theory as needed with new lemmas. Here we present a particular proof theory for 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT}. Notice that even though the lemmas are written in an inference rule format, they should be read as “if the premises are true, then the conclusions are true”, i.e., not an inductive definition.

In Figure 4, we present a collection of lemmas that is useful for complexity analysis. They can be grouped roughly by the type constructor involved, resulting in the usual formation, introduction, and elimination rules. For brevity, we write the rules in the local form; however, all rules (with the exception of Lemma 6.14, 6.16, and 6.17) can be interpreted to have an ambient context prepended to the judgments.

6.1 Universes

The introduction rules for 𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i\mathtt{Univ}_{i} are the formation rules for the “small types” ( Lemma 6.6, 6.18, 6.12, 6.15, 6.21). These introduction rules capture the by-name evaluation behavior of elements of the universe; consequently, there is no cost-aware version of the typecase mechanism.

Lemma 6.1 (Universe formation).


𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i≐𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i∈0𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i+1\mathtt{Univ}_{i}\doteq\mathtt{Univ}_{i}\in_{0}\mathtt{Univ}_{i+1} for all ii.

Proof.

First, we need to show there is a ϕ\phi such that 𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i+1∼𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i+1↓ϕ∈τω\mathtt{Univ}_{i+1}\sim\mathtt{Univ}_{i+1}\downarrow\phi\in\tau_{\omega}. By definition, τω=Types​(vω,τω)\tau_{\omega}=\text{Types}(v_{\omega},\tau_{\omega}) and Univ​(vω)⊆Types​(vω,τω)\text{Univ}(v_{\omega})\subseteq\text{Types}(v_{\omega},\tau_{\omega}), so it suffices to show 𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i+1∼𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i+1↓ϕ∈vω\mathtt{Univ}_{i+1}\sim\mathtt{Univ}_{i+1}\downarrow\phi\in v_{\omega} for some ϕ\phi. By definition of vωv_{\omega}, take ϕ={(A,B)∣∃α.τi+1(A,B,α)}\phi=\{(A,B)\mid\exists\alpha.\,\tau_{i+1}(A,B,\alpha)\}.

Next, we need to show ϕ⁡(𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i,𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i)\phi(\mathtt{Univ}_{i},\mathtt{Univ}_{i}). It suffices to show there is α\alpha such that τi+1​(𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i,𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i,α)\tau_{i+1}(\mathtt{Univ}_{i},\mathtt{Univ}_{i},\alpha). Since τi+1=Types​(vi+1,τi+1)\tau_{i+1}=\text{Types}(v_{i+1},\tau_{i+1}), it suffices to show 𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i∼𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i↓α∈vi+1\mathtt{Univ}_{i}\sim\mathtt{Univ}_{i}\downarrow\alpha\in v_{i+1}. By definition of vi+1v_{i+1}, it suffices to take α={(A,B)∣∃β.τi(A,B,β)}\alpha=\{(A,B)\mid\exists\beta.\,\tau_{i}(A,B,\beta)\}. ∎

The introduction rules for 𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i\mathtt{Univ}_{i} are the formation rules for the type constructors.

Lemma 6.2 (Universe elimination).

If

  1. 1.

    A≐A′∈𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟iA\doteq A^{\prime}\in\mathtt{Univ}_{i}

then A≐A′​𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾A\doteq A^{\prime}\;\mathsf{type}.

Proof.

We need to show A∼A′↓α∈τωA\sim A^{\prime}\downarrow\alpha\in\tau_{\omega} for some α\alpha. By assumption, A∼A′∈⟦𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i⟧A\sim A^{\prime}\in\llbracket\mathtt{Univ}_{i}\rrbracket. By definition,

⟦𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i⟧={(A,B)∣∃α.τi(A,B,α)}\llbracket\mathtt{Univ}_{i}\rrbracket=\{(A,B)\mid\exists\alpha.\,\tau_{i}(A,B,\alpha)\}

Hence A∼A′↓α∈τiA\sim A^{\prime}\downarrow\alpha\in\tau_{i} for some α\alpha, and so the result holds by Lemma 4.10. ∎

6.2 Equality

Lemma 6.3 (Equality formation).

If

  1. 1.

    A≐A′∈𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟iA\doteq A^{\prime}\in\mathtt{Univ}_{i}

  2. 2.

    M≐M′∈AM\doteq M^{\prime}\in A

  3. 3.

    N≐N′∈AN\doteq N^{\prime}\in A

then 𝚎𝚚A(M,N)≐𝚎𝚚A′(M′,N′)∈0𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i\mathtt{eq}_{A}(M,\allowbreak N)\doteq\mathtt{eq}_{A^{\prime}}(M^{\prime},\allowbreak N^{\prime})\in_{0}\mathtt{Univ}_{i}

Proof.

By definition, ⟦𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i⟧={(A,B)∣∃ϕ.τi(A,B,ϕ)}\llbracket\mathtt{Univ}_{i}\rrbracket=\{(A,B)\mid\exists\phi.\,\tau_{i}(A,B,\phi)\}, so we need to show τi​(𝚎𝚚A​(M,N),𝚎𝚚A′​(M′,N′),ϕ)\tau_{i}(\mathtt{eq}_{A}(M,\allowbreak N),\mathtt{eq}_{A^{\prime}}(M^{\prime},\allowbreak N^{\prime}),\phi) for some ϕ\phi. Since τi=Types​(vi,τi)\tau_{i}=\text{Types}(v_{i},\tau_{i}), it suffices to show Eq​(τi)​(𝚎𝚚A​(M,N),𝚎𝚚A′​(M′,N′),ϕ)\text{Eq}(\tau_{i})(\mathtt{eq}_{A}(M,\allowbreak N),\mathtt{eq}_{A^{\prime}}(M^{\prime},\allowbreak N^{\prime}),\phi). By assumption and definition of ⟦𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i⟧\llbracket\mathtt{Univ}_{i}\rrbracket, we have A∼A↓α∈τiA\sim A\downarrow\alpha\in\tau_{i} for some α\alpha. Furthermore, by Lemma 4.10 and unicity of τω\tau_{\omega}, we have

  1. 1.

    M∼M′∈αM\sim M^{\prime}\in\alpha

  2. 2.

    N∼N′∈αN\sim N^{\prime}\in\alpha

So the result holds by taking ϕ={(⋆,⋆)∣M∼N∈α}\phi=\{(\star,\star)\mid M\sim N\in\alpha\}. ∎

Lemma 6.4 (Equality introduction).

If

  1. 1.

    M≐N∈AM\doteq N\in A

then ⋆≐⋆∈0𝚎𝚚A(M,N)\star\doteq\star\in_{0}\mathtt{eq}_{A}(M,\allowbreak N).

Proof.

First, we need to show 𝚎𝚚A​(M,N)∼𝚎𝚚A​(M,N)↓ϕ∈τω\mathtt{eq}_{A}(M,\allowbreak N)\sim\mathtt{eq}_{A}(M,\allowbreak N)\downarrow\phi\in\tau_{\omega} for some ϕ\phi, which holds by Lemma 6.3. By definition, ϕ={(⋆,⋆)∣M∼N∈⟦A⟧}\phi=\{(\star,\star)\mid M\sim N\in\llbracket A\rrbracket\}. Next, we need to show ϕ⁡(⋆,⋆)\phi(\star,\star). It suffices to show M∼N∈⟦A⟧M\sim N\in\llbracket A\rrbracket, which holds by assumption. ∎

Lemma 6.5 (Equality elimination).

If

  1. 1.

    P≐P′∈𝚎𝚚A​(M,N)P\doteq P^{\prime}\in\mathtt{eq}_{A}(M,\allowbreak N)

then M≐N∈AM\doteq N\in A.

Proof.

First, we need to show A∼A↓α∈τωA\sim A\downarrow\alpha\in\tau_{\omega}. By assumption, we have 𝚎𝚚A​(M,N)∼𝚎𝚚A​(M,N)↓ϕ∈τω\mathtt{eq}_{A}(M,\allowbreak N)\sim\mathtt{eq}_{A}(M,\allowbreak N)\downarrow\phi\in\tau_{\omega} for some ϕ\phi. This implies A∼A↓α∈τωA\sim A\downarrow\alpha\in\tau_{\omega}. By unicity, we have ϕ={(⋆,⋆)∣M∼N∈α}\phi=\{(\star,\star)\mid M\sim N\in\alpha\}. It remains to show M∼N∈αM\sim N\in\alpha. By assumption, P∼P′∈ϕP\sim P^{\prime}\in\phi, so we have M∼N∈αM\sim N\in\alpha, as required. ∎

6.3 Nat

Before introducing judgments involving complexities, we need to prove some lemmas governing the construction and use of natural numbers. As we alluded to in section 2, the complexity component of a judgment is simply a natural number in the programming language itself. Aside from the rules for eliminating foreign functions, there are also two elimination rules – Lemma 6.10 is the ordinary eliminator, and Lemma 6.11 is the eliminator that additionally tracks the complexity of the case analysis given the complexity of each branch. Note that there is no syntactic form for the recursor: it is an instance of general recursion. The associated induction rule is also an instance of the elimination rule for the funtime type (see Lemma 6.23 and 6.24).

Lemma 6.6 (Nat formation).


𝚗𝚊𝚝≐𝚗𝚊𝚝∈0𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i\mathtt{nat}\doteq\mathtt{nat}\in_{0}\mathtt{Univ}_{i}.

Proof.

By definition of ⟦𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i⟧\llbracket\mathtt{Univ}_{i}\rrbracket, it suffices to show τi​(𝚗𝚊𝚝,𝚗𝚊𝚝,α)\tau_{i}(\mathtt{nat},\mathtt{nat},\alpha) for some α\alpha. Unfolding definitions, we have Nat​(τi)⊆Types​(vω,τi)=τi\text{Nat}(\tau_{i})\subseteq\text{Types}(v_{\omega},\tau_{i})=\tau_{i}. So take α=ω\alpha=\omega, since Nat​(τi)​(𝚗𝚊𝚝,𝚗𝚊𝚝,ω)\text{Nat}(\tau_{i})(\mathtt{nat},\mathtt{nat},\omega). ∎

Lemma 6.7 (Nat introduction).
  1. 1.

    𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘≐𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘∈𝚗𝚊𝚝{\mathtt{zero}}\doteq{\mathtt{zero}}\in\mathtt{nat}.

  2. 2.

    If M≐M′∈𝚗𝚊𝚝M\doteq M^{\prime}\in\mathtt{nat}, then 𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(M)≐𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(M′)∈𝚗𝚊𝚝{\mathtt{suc}}(M)\doteq{\mathtt{suc}}(M^{\prime})\in\mathtt{nat}.

Proof.

First, by Lemma 6.6, we know there is α\alpha such that 𝚗𝚊𝚝∼𝚗𝚊𝚝↓α∈τ\mathtt{nat}\sim\mathtt{nat}\downarrow\alpha\in\tau. By unicity of τω\tau_{\omega}, α=ω\alpha=\omega. For part 1, it suffices to show 𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘∼𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘∈ω{\mathtt{zero}}\sim{\mathtt{zero}}\in\omega. This holds by definition, as ω={(𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘,𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘)}∪{(𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(V),𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(V′))∣ω⁡(V,V′)}\omega=\{({\mathtt{zero}},{\mathtt{zero}})\}\cup\{({\mathtt{suc}}(V),{\mathtt{suc}}(V^{\prime}))\mid\omega(V,V^{\prime})\}. Now suppose M≐M′∈𝚗𝚊𝚝M\doteq M^{\prime}\in\mathtt{nat}, which by above, means M∼M′∈ωM\sim M^{\prime}\in\omega. We need to show 𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(M)∼𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(M′)∈𝚗𝚊𝚝{\mathtt{suc}}(M)\sim{\mathtt{suc}}(M^{\prime})\in\mathtt{nat}. By assumption, M⇓VM\Downarrow V, M′⇓V′M^{\prime}\Downarrow V^{\prime}, and ω⁡(V,V′)\omega(V,V^{\prime}). Hence 𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(M)⇓𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(V){\mathtt{suc}}(M)\Downarrow{\mathtt{suc}}(V) and 𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(M′)⇓𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(V′){\mathtt{suc}}(M^{\prime})\Downarrow{\mathtt{suc}}(V^{\prime}). By definition, ω⁡(𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(V),𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(V′))\omega({\mathtt{suc}}(V),{\mathtt{suc}}(V^{\prime})), and so 𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(M)∼𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(M′)∈𝚗𝚊𝚝{\mathtt{suc}}(M)\sim{\mathtt{suc}}(M^{\prime})\in\mathtt{nat}. ∎

Lemma 6.8 (FF elimination (1)).
  1. 1.

    If f:ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} and M≐M′∈𝚗𝚊𝚝M\doteq M^{\prime}\in\mathtt{nat}, then f^⁡(M)≐f^⁡(M′)∈𝚗𝚊𝚝\mathop{\hat{f}}(M)\doteq\mathop{\hat{f}}(M^{\prime})\in\mathtt{nat}.

  2. 2.

    If f:ℕ→ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} and M1≐M1′∈𝚗𝚊𝚝M_{1}\doteq M_{1}^{\prime}\in\mathtt{nat} and M2≐M2′∈𝚗𝚊𝚝M_{2}\doteq M_{2}^{\prime}\in\mathtt{nat}, then (M1f^M2)≐(M1′f^M2′)∈𝚗𝚊𝚝(M_{1}\mathbin{\widehat{f}}M_{2})\doteq(M_{1}^{\prime}\mathbin{\widehat{f}}M_{2}^{\prime})\in\mathtt{nat}.

Proof.

We prove the unary case, as the binary case follows similarly. Since 𝚗𝚊𝚝∼𝚗𝚊𝚝↓ω∈τω\mathtt{nat}\sim\mathtt{nat}\downarrow\omega\in\tau_{\omega}, it suffices to show f^⁡(M)∼f^⁡(M′)∈ω\mathop{\hat{f}}(M)\sim\mathop{\hat{f}}(M^{\prime})\in\omega. By assumption and Lemma 5.11, we know M⇓VM\Downarrow V, M′⇓V′M^{\prime}\Downarrow V^{\prime}, and ω⁡(V,V′)\omega(V,V^{\prime}). This means V=m¯V=\bar{m} and V′=m¯V^{\prime}=\bar{m} for some mm. Hence,

f^⁡(M)\displaystyle\mathop{\hat{f}}(M) ↦f^∗⁡(m¯)↦f⁡(m)¯\displaystyle\mapsto^{*}\mathop{\hat{f}}(\bar{m})\mapsto\overline{f(m)}
f^⁡(M′)\displaystyle\mathop{\hat{f}}(M^{\prime}) ↦f^∗⁡(m¯)↦f⁡(m)¯\displaystyle\mapsto^{*}\mathop{\hat{f}}(\bar{m})\mapsto\overline{f(m)}

By Lemma 4.1, it suffices to show f⁡(m)¯∼f⁡(m)¯∈ω\overline{f(m)}\sim\overline{f(m)}\in\omega, which holds by definition of ω\omega. ∎

Lemma 6.9 (FF elimination (2)).
  1. 1.

    If f:ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} and V≐V′∈0𝚗𝚊𝚝V\doteq V^{\prime}\in_{0}\mathtt{nat}, then f^⁡(V)≐f^⁡(V′)∈𝚗𝚊𝚝⁡[1¯]\mathop{\hat{f}}(V)\doteq\mathop{\hat{f}}(V^{\prime})\in\mathtt{nat}{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[\bar{1}]}} .

  2. 2.

    If f:ℕ→ℕ→ℕf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} and V1≐V1′∈0𝚗𝚊𝚝V_{1}\doteq V_{1}^{\prime}\in_{0}\mathtt{nat} and V2≐V2′∈0𝚗𝚊𝚝V_{2}\doteq V_{2}^{\prime}\in_{0}\mathtt{nat}, then (V1f^V2)≐(V1′f^V2′)∈𝚗𝚊𝚝⁡[1¯](V_{1}\mathbin{\widehat{f}}V_{2})\doteq(V_{1}^{\prime}\mathbin{\widehat{f}}V_{2}^{\prime})\in\mathtt{nat}{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[\bar{1}]}} .

Proof.

Similar to proof of Lemma 6.8. ∎

Lemma 6.10 (Nat elimination (1)).

If

  1. 1.

    a:𝚗𝚊𝚝≫A∈𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟ia{:}\mathtt{nat}\gg A\in\mathtt{Univ}_{i},

  2. 2.

    M≐M′∈𝚗𝚊𝚝M\doteq M^{\prime}\in\mathtt{nat},

  3. 3.

    p:𝚎𝚚𝚗𝚊𝚝​(𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘,M)≫M0≐M0′∈[𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘/a]​Ap{:}\mathtt{eq}_{\mathtt{nat}}({\mathtt{zero}},\allowbreak M)\gg M_{0}\doteq M_{0}^{\prime}\in[{\mathtt{zero}}/a]A,

  4. 4.

    a:𝚗𝚊𝚝,p:𝚎𝚚𝚗𝚊𝚝​(𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(a),M)≫M1≐M1′∈[𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(a)/a]​Aa{:}\mathtt{nat},p{:}\mathtt{eq}_{\mathtt{nat}}({\mathtt{suc}}(a),\allowbreak M)\gg M_{1}\doteq M_{1}^{\prime}\in[{\mathtt{suc}}(a)/a]A,

then 𝚒𝚏𝚣(M){M0;a.M1}≐𝚒𝚏𝚣(M′){M0′;a.M1′}∈⟨M/a⟩A\mathtt{ifz}(M)\{M_{0};a.M_{1}\}\doteq\mathtt{ifz}(M^{\prime})\{M_{0}^{\prime};a.M_{1}^{\prime}\}\in\left<M/a\right>A.

Proof.

By assumption 2, M∼M′∈ωM\sim M^{\prime}\in\omega, so

  1. 1.

    M⇓VM\Downarrow V

  2. 2.

    M′⇓V′M^{\prime}\Downarrow V^{\prime}

  3. 3.

    ω⁡(V,V′)\omega(V,V^{\prime})

One possibility is that (V,V′)=(𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘,𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘)(V,V^{\prime})=({\mathtt{zero}},{\mathtt{zero}}). In this case, we know that

𝚒𝚏𝚣(M){M0;a.M1}\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz}(M)\{M_{0};a.M_{1}\} ↦∗𝚒𝚏𝚣(𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘){M0;a.M1}↦M0\displaystyle\mapsto^{*}\mathtt{ifz}({\mathtt{zero}})\{M_{0};a.M_{1}\}\mapsto M_{0}
𝚒𝚏𝚣(M′){M0′;a.M1′}\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz}(M^{\prime})\{M_{0}^{\prime};a.M_{1}^{\prime}\} ↦∗𝚒𝚏𝚣(𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘){M0′;a.M1′}↦M0′\displaystyle\mapsto^{*}\mathtt{ifz}({\mathtt{zero}})\{M_{0}^{\prime};a.M_{1}^{\prime}\}\mapsto M_{0}^{\prime}

By Lemma 5.3, it suffices to show M0≐M0′∈[𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘/a]​AM_{0}\doteq M_{0}^{\prime}\in[{\mathtt{zero}}/a]A, which holds by the third assumption, given that we show 𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘≐M∈0𝚗𝚊𝚝{\mathtt{zero}}{}\doteq M\in_{0}\mathtt{nat}, which again follows from Lemma 5.3. The other possibility is that (V,V′)=(𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(U),𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(U′))(V,V^{\prime})=({\mathtt{suc}}(U),{\mathtt{suc}}(U^{\prime})) where ω⁡(U,U′)\omega(U,U^{\prime}). Then we have

𝚒𝚏𝚣(M){M0;a.M1}\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz}(M)\{M_{0};a.M_{1}\} ↦∗𝚒𝚏𝚣(𝚜𝚞𝚌(U)){M0;a.M1}↦[U/a]M1\displaystyle\mapsto^{*}\mathtt{ifz}({\mathtt{suc}}(U))\{M_{0};a.M_{1}\}\mapsto[U/a]M_{1}
𝚒𝚏𝚣(M′){M0′;a.M1′}\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz}(M^{\prime})\{M_{0}^{\prime};a.M_{1}^{\prime}\} ↦∗𝚒𝚏𝚣(𝚜𝚞𝚌(U′)){M0′;a.M1′}↦[U′/a]M1′\displaystyle\mapsto^{*}\mathtt{ifz}({\mathtt{suc}}(U^{\prime}))\{M_{0}^{\prime};a.M_{1}^{\prime}\}\mapsto[U^{\prime}/a]M_{1}^{\prime}

By Lemma 5.3, it suffices to show [U/a]​M1≐[U′/a]​M1′∈[𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(U)/a]​A[U/a]M_{1}\doteq[U^{\prime}/a]M_{1}^{\prime}\in[{\mathtt{suc}}(U)/a]A, which holds by the fourth assumption, given we show that P∈0𝚎𝚚𝚗𝚊𝚝(𝚜𝚞𝚌(U),M)P\in_{0}\mathtt{eq}_{\mathtt{nat}}({\mathtt{suc}}(U),\allowbreak M) for some PP. By Lemma 6.4, it suffices to show 𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(U)≐M∈𝚗𝚊𝚝{\mathtt{suc}}(U)\doteq M\in\mathtt{nat}, which holds by Lemma 5.3. ∎

Lemma 6.11 (Nat elimination (2)).

If

  1. 1.

    a:𝚗𝚊𝚝≫A∈𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟ia{:}\mathtt{nat}\gg A\in\mathtt{Univ}_{i},

  2. 2.

    V≐V′∈0𝚗𝚊𝚝V\doteq V^{\prime}\in_{0}\mathtt{nat},

  3. 3.

    P0≐P0∈𝚗𝚊𝚝P_{0}\doteq P_{0}\in\mathtt{nat},

  4. 4.

    a:𝚗𝚊𝚝≫P1≐P1∈𝚗𝚊𝚝a{:}\mathtt{nat}\gg P_{1}\doteq P_{1}\in\mathtt{nat},

  5. 5.

    p:𝚎𝚚𝚗𝚊𝚝​(𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘,V)≫M0≐M0′∈[𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘/a]​A​[P0]p{:}\mathtt{eq}_{\mathtt{nat}}({\mathtt{zero}},\allowbreak V)\gg M_{0}\doteq M_{0}^{\prime}\in[{\mathtt{zero}}/a]A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P_{0}]}},

  6. 6.

    a:𝚗𝚊𝚝,p:𝚎𝚚𝚗𝚊𝚝​(𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(a),V)≫M1≐M1′∈[𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(a)/a]​A​[P1]a{:}\mathtt{nat},p{:}\mathtt{eq}_{\mathtt{nat}}({\mathtt{suc}}(a),\allowbreak V)\gg M_{1}\doteq M_{1}^{\prime}\in[{\mathtt{suc}}(a)/a]A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P_{1}]}},

then 𝚒𝚏𝚣(V){M0;a.M1}≐𝚒𝚏𝚣(V′){M0′;a.M1′}∈[V/a]A[𝚒𝚏𝚣(V){𝚜𝚞𝚌(P0);a.𝚜𝚞𝚌(P1)}]\mathtt{ifz}(V)\{M_{0};a.M_{1}\}\doteq\mathtt{ifz}(V^{\prime})\{M_{0}^{\prime};a.M_{1}^{\prime}\}\in[V/a]A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[\mathtt{ifz}(V)\{{\mathtt{suc}}(P_{0});a.{\mathtt{suc}}(P_{1})\}]}} .

Proof.

By assumption 2, we know ω⁡(V,V′)\omega(V,V^{\prime}). One possibility is that (V,V′)=(𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘,𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘)(V,V^{\prime})=({\mathtt{zero}},{\mathtt{zero}}). In this case, we know that

𝚒𝚏𝚣(𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘){M0;a.M1}\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz}({\mathtt{zero}})\{M_{0};a.M_{1}\} ↦M0\displaystyle\mapsto M_{0}
𝚒𝚏𝚣(𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘′){M0′;a.M1′}\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz}({\mathtt{zero}}^{\prime})\{M_{0}^{\prime};a.M_{1}^{\prime}\} ↦M0′\displaystyle\mapsto M_{0}^{\prime}
𝚒𝚏𝚣(𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘){𝚜𝚞𝚌(P0);a.𝚜𝚞𝚌(P1)}\displaystyle\mathtt{ifz}({\mathtt{zero}})\{{\mathtt{suc}}(P_{0});a.{\mathtt{suc}}(P_{1})\} ↦∗𝚜𝚞𝚌(P0)\displaystyle\mapsto^{*}{\mathtt{suc}}(P_{0})

By Lemma 5.3, we have 𝚒𝚏𝚣(M){𝚜𝚞𝚌(P0);a.𝚜𝚞𝚌(P1)}≐𝚜𝚞𝚌(P0)∈𝚗𝚊𝚝\mathtt{ifz}(M)\{{\mathtt{suc}}(P_{0});a.{\mathtt{suc}}(P_{1})\}\doteq{\mathtt{suc}}(P_{0})\in\mathtt{nat}. So by Lemma 5.3, it suffices to show M0≐M0′∈[𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘/a]​A​[P0]M_{0}\doteq M_{0}^{\prime}\in[{\mathtt{zero}}/a]A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P_{0}]}} . This holds by assumption 5, given that we show 𝚣𝚎𝚛𝚘≐V∈0𝚗𝚊𝚝{\mathtt{zero}}\doteq V\in_{0}\mathtt{nat}, which holds by Lemma 6.7. The other possibility is that (V,V′)=(𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(U),𝚜𝚞𝚌⁡(U′))(V,V^{\prime})=({\mathtt{suc}}(U),{\mathtt{suc}}(U^{\prime})) where ω⁡(U,U′)\omega(U,U^{\prime}). Then we have

6.5 Relations

Some properties about natural numbers can be lifted from the metatheory. Given a relation r:𝒫⁡(ℕ×ℕ)r:\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}), Mr^NM\mathrel{\widehat{r}}N is the internal representation of r⁡(m,n)r(m,n) when M⇓m¯M\Downarrow\bar{m} and N⇓n¯N\Downarrow\bar{n}. For the following lemmas, we just prove the binary versions, noting that the proof stays the same for any relation 𝒫⁡(ℕk)\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}^{k}) of fixed arity kk.

As for subsets, the rules for relations cannot be generalized to arbitrary contexts in the expected way. The introduction rule (Lemma 6.16) involves identifying metatheoretic numbers that represent closed theoretic natural numbers. This is not possible for open terms of type 𝚗𝚊𝚝\mathtt{nat}. The elimination rule (Lemma 6.17) has a similar problem. As in the case for subsets, we just instantiate the semantics involving open judgments for relations.

Lemma 6.15 (Relation Formation).

If

  1. 1.

    r:𝒫⁡(ℕ×ℕ)r:\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N})

  2. 2.

    M≐M′∈𝚗𝚊𝚝M\doteq M^{\prime}\in\mathtt{nat}

  3. 3.

    N≐N′∈𝚗𝚊𝚝N\doteq N^{\prime}\in\mathtt{nat}

then Mr^N≐M′r^N′∈0𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟iM\mathrel{\widehat{r}}N\doteq M^{\prime}\mathrel{\widehat{r}}N^{\prime}\in_{0}\mathtt{Univ}_{i}.

Proof.

By definition of ⟦𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i⟧\llbracket\mathtt{Univ}_{i}\rrbracket, we need to show τi​(Mr^N,M′r^N′,ϕ)\tau_{i}(M\mathrel{\widehat{r}}N,M^{\prime}\mathrel{\widehat{r}}N^{\prime},\phi) for some ϕ\phi. By definition, τi=Types​(vi,τi)\tau_{i}=\text{Types}(v_{i},\tau_{i}), so it suffices to show Rel2​(τi)​(Mr^N,M′r^N′,ϕ)\text{Rel2}(\tau_{i})(M\mathrel{\widehat{r}}N,M^{\prime}\mathrel{\widehat{r}}N^{\prime},\phi) for some ϕ\phi. By assumption and unicity of τω\tau_{\omega}, we know M∼M′∈ωM\sim M^{\prime}\in\omega and N∼N′∈ωN\sim N^{\prime}\in\omega, so by definition, take ϕ={(⋆,⋆)∣∃m,n.r(m,n)∧M∼m¯∈ω∧N∼n¯∈ω}\phi=\{(\star,\star)\mid\exists m,n.\,r(m,n)\land M\sim\bar{m}\in\omega\land N\sim\bar{n}\in\omega\}. ∎

Lemma 6.16 (Relation introduction).

If

  1. 1.

    M≐m¯∈𝚗𝚊𝚝M\doteq\bar{m}\in\mathtt{nat} for some mm

  2. 2.

    N≐n¯∈𝚗𝚊𝚝N\doteq\bar{n}\in\mathtt{nat} for some nn

  3. 3.

    r⁡(m,n)r(m,n)

then ⋆≐⋆∈0Mr^N\star\doteq\star\in_{0}M\mathrel{\widehat{r}}N.

Proof.

First, we need to show Mr^N∼Mr^N↓ϕ∈τωM\mathrel{\widehat{r}}N\sim M\mathrel{\widehat{r}}N\downarrow\phi\in\tau_{\omega} for some ϕ\phi, which holds by Lemma 6.15. By unicity,

ϕ={(⋆,⋆)∣∃m,n.r(m,n)∧M∼m¯∈ω∧N∼n¯∈ω}\phi=\{(\star,\star)\mid\exists m,n.\,r(m,n)\land M\sim\bar{m}\in\omega\land N\sim\bar{n}\in\omega\}

If

  1. 1.

ϕ={(⋆,⋆)∣∃m,n.r(m,n)∧M∼m¯∈ω∧N∼n¯∈ω}\phi=\{(\star,\star)\mid\exists m,n.\,r(m,n)\land M\sim\bar{m}\in\omega\land N\sim\bar{n}\in\omega\}

6.7 Funtime

Now we have all the ingredients to introduce the new dependent function type constructor “funtime” that internalizes the complexity-aware membership judgment Γ≫M∈A⁡[P]\Gamma\gg M\in A{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[P]}}.

Lemma 6.21 (Funtime formation).

If

  1. 1.

    A≐A′∈𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟iA\doteq A^{\prime}\in\mathtt{Univ}_{i}

  2. 2.

    a:A≫B≐B′∈𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟ia{:}A\gg B\doteq B^{\prime}\in\mathtt{Univ}_{i}

  3. 3.

    a:A≫P≐P′∈𝚗𝚊𝚝a{:}A\gg P\doteq P^{\prime}\in\mathtt{nat}

then a:A→B[P]≐a:A′→B′[P′]∈0𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚟i{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{a{:}A\to B}}{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{[P]}}\doteq{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{a{:}A^{\prime}\to B^{\prime}}}{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{[P^{\prime}]}}\in_{0}\mathtt{Univ}_{i}.

Proof.

Before we prove the introduction rule, we will need some auxiliary definitions:

  1. 1.

    Let the domain of a PER α\alpha be |α|={V∣α⁡(V,V)}\left|\alpha\right|=\{V\mid\alpha(V,V)\}.

  2. 2.

  3. 3.

    Given a:α​⊳​P∼P∈ωa{:}\alpha\rhd P\sim P\in\omega and V1,V2:|α|V_{1},V_{2}:\left|\alpha\right|, write V1⋖a:α.PV2V_{1}\lessdot_{a{:}\alpha.P}V_{2} when ma:α.PV1<ma:α.PV2m_{a{:}\alpha.P}V_{1}<m_{a{:}\alpha.P}V_{2}.

Lemma 6.22.

Given a set AA and a function f:A→ℕf:A\to\mathbb{N}, (A,≺)(A,\prec) is well-founded, where a≺b⇔f⁡(a)<f⁡(b)a\prec b\iff f(a)<f(b).

Proof.

Suppose S⊆AS\subseteq A is inductive: ∀x∈A,(∀y∈A,y≺x⟹y∈S)⟹x∈S\forall x\in A,(\forall y\in A,y\prec x\implies y\in S)\implies x\in S. It suffices to show S=AS=A, and hence it suffices to show A⊆SA\subseteq S. Suppose x∈Ax\in A. By assumption, it suffices to show

∀y∈A,y≺x⟹y∈S⇔∀y∈A,f⁡(y)<f⁡(x)⟹y∈S\forall y\in A,y\prec x\implies y\in S\iff\forall y\in A,f(y)<f(x)\implies y\in S

Proceed by induction on f⁡(x)f(x). If f⁡(x)=0f(x)=0, then the result holds vacuously. Otherwise, let f⁡(x)=mf(x)=m, and suppose y∈Ay\in A and f⁡(y)<mf(y)<m. We need to show y∈Sy\in S. By the assumption that SS inductive, it suffices to show

∀z∈A,f⁡(z)<f⁡(y)⟹z∈S\forall z\in A,f(z)<f(y)\implies z\in S

which holds by induction. ∎

Corollary 6.22.1.

Given a:α​⊳​P∼P∈ωa{:}\alpha\rhd P\sim P\in\omega , (|α|,⋖a:α.P)(\left|\alpha\right|,\lessdot_{a{:}\alpha.P}) is a well-founded set.

As foreshadowed in the introduction, the proof for the introduction rule proceeds by induction on the well-founded ordering on the inputs to the recursive calls. We conjecture that that this rule is sufficient for verifying all first-order functions. Curried functions and closures present problems in some situations because the first argument does not necessarily decrease in a partial function application. One possible solution to this would be to define an ordering on the resulting closure and demand that partial applications induce a “smaller” closure in an appropriate sense. We leave this for future explorations.

7 Machines

So far, we have considered a straightforward model of computation where each transition of the operation semantics is assigned unit cost. Now, we extend the operational semantics with additional primitive forms of computation that are assigned unit cost. This is similar to the instruction set of physical machines and represent operations that are considered to be unit cost with the justification that they are usually implemented efficiently in practice. Without these primitives, addition and multiplication defined internally would have linear and super-linear complexities, which seemingly goes against common intuition. The crux of the issue is that these operations have essentially constant time complexity, under the assumption that the inputs fit within the word size of a given machine. Hence, we index the operational semantics with a parameter ww representing the word size and introduce primitives that operate on word-sized inputs.

Transition becomes a family of relations _↦w_:𝒫(𝖤𝗑𝗉×𝖤𝗑𝗉)\_\mapsto_{w}\_:\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{Exp}\times\mathsf{Exp}) over the parameter w:ℕw:\mathbb{N}, the maximum value of a number that fits in the word size. There are new syntactic forms f†⁡M\mathop{f^{\dagger}}M and Mf†NM\mathbin{f^{\dagger}}N representing unary and binary arithmetic operators on natural numbers, respectively. They have the following associated transition steps:

E↦E′f†⁡E↦f†⁡E′​m<wf†⁡m¯↦f⁡(m)¯​E1↦E1′E1f†E2↦E1′f†E1​V​𝗏𝖺𝗅E2↦E2′E1f†E2↦E1f†E2′​m,n<wm¯f†n¯↦f⁡(m,n)¯\frac{E\mapsto E^{\prime}}{\mathop{f^{\dagger}}E\mapsto\mathop{f^{\dagger}}E^{\prime}}\par\frac{m<w}{\mathop{f^{\dagger}}\bar{m}\mapsto\overline{f(m)}}\par\frac{E_{1}\mapsto E_{1}^{\prime}}{E_{1}\mathbin{f^{\dagger}}E_{2}\mapsto E_{1}^{\prime}\mathbin{f^{\dagger}}E_{1}}\par\frac{V\;\mathsf{val}\quad E_{2}\mapsto E_{2}^{\prime}}{E_{1}\mathbin{f^{\dagger}}E_{2}\mapsto E_{1}\mathbin{f^{\dagger}}E_{2}^{\prime}}\par\frac{m,n<w}{\bar{m}\mathbin{f^{\dagger}}\bar{n}\mapsto\overline{f(m,n)}}

In the beta rules, inputs to the operator are required to fit in one word. What is “reasonably” primitive depends on the particular machine one has in mind, but we will postulate that ff can be addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulus.

Note that while we already have a foreign function interface via f^⁡(M)\mathop{\hat{f}}(M) and (Mf^N)(M\mathbin{\widehat{f}}N), these are intended to be used in the cost expressions and not programs. As such, the the foreign function interface has no restriction on the inputs to the operators, and when subjected to complexity verification, invocation of the interface should be thought of as functions calls to an “oracle” that can compute any function in constant time. This is useful when one is interested in a more abstract measure of cost, such as the number of recursive calls a function makes as opposed to the actual running time of said function.

There is a new associated elimination rule for primitive computations on natural numbers:

Lemma 7.1 (Primitive elimination).

If

  1. 1.

    If V≐V′∈0𝚗𝚊𝚝V\doteq V^{\prime}\in_{0}\mathtt{nat} and P∈V<^w¯P\in V\mathrel{\widehat{<}}\bar{w}, then f†⁡V≐f†⁡V′∈𝚗𝚊𝚝⁡[1¯]\mathop{f^{\dagger}}V\doteq\mathop{f^{\dagger}}V^{\prime}\in\mathtt{nat}{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[\bar{1}]}} .

  2. 2.

    If V≐V′∈0𝚗𝚊𝚝V\doteq V^{\prime}\in_{0}\mathtt{nat}, U≐U′∈0𝚗𝚊𝚝U\doteq U^{\prime}\in_{0}\mathtt{nat}, P∈V<^w¯P\in V\mathrel{\widehat{<}}\bar{w}, Q∈U<^w¯Q\in U\mathrel{\widehat{<}}\bar{w}, then Vf†U≐Vf†U∈𝚗𝚊𝚝⁡[1¯]V\mathbin{f^{\dagger}}U\doteq V\mathbin{f^{\dagger}}U\in\mathtt{nat}{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}{\;[\bar{1}]}} .

Proof.

Similar to proof of Lemma 6.8. ∎

8 Example: greatest common divisor

We are now equipped to state and analyze the computational complexity for a general class of programs. We focus on analyzing the complexity of Euclid’s algorithm for computing the gcd of two natural numbers. This is a prototypical example of an algorithm which is not structurally recursive, and we demonstrate that the semantic framework of 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT} is capable of handling such recursive constructions.

Remark.

For presentation purposes, we derive a basic bound and acknowledge that it’s not the tightest characterization. It is certainly possible to carry out a more detailed analysis in 𝐂𝐀𝐓𝐓\mathbf{CATT}.

Let the ternary predicate gcdProp:𝒫⁡(ℕ×ℕ×ℕ)\textit{gcdProp}:\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}) be defined as gcd​(d,m,n)\textit{gcd}(d,m,n) if dd is the gcd of mm and nn. This is then internalized as g​c​d​P​r​o​p^⁡(D,M,N)\mathop{\widehat{gcdProp}}(D,M,N) for D,M,N∈𝚗𝚊𝚝D,M,N\in\mathtt{nat}. It is possible to define this predicate internally, but it is convenient to delegate this routine verification to the metatheory. Let the gcd algorithm be defined as follows:

9 Parallelism

So far we have developed a computational type theory for analyzing the computational complexity of sequential computations. To extend the theory to account for parallel programs, we arrange the operational semantics so that each transition step corresponds to one unit of cost in the span of the computation. The idea is that sub-terms of a computation that are independent of each other transition simultaneously whenever possible. Intuitively, the resulting cost measures the length of the longest sequence of dependencies in the computation. Figure 6 contains selected rules of the parallel operational semantics of 𝐏𝐋\mathbf{PL}. The omitted rules remain the same from the sequential operational semantics. The unary sequential composition is generalized to the binary sequencing operator 𝚙𝚊𝚛(E1;E2;a.b.E3)\mathtt{par}(E_{1};E_{2};a.b.E_{3}), which transitions E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} simultaneously and binds the results to aa and bb for use in E3E_{3}. Binary sequencing can be taken as a primitive. Here we define it in terms of unary sequencing:

𝚙𝚊𝚛(E1;E2;a.b.E3)≜𝚕𝚎𝚝c=⟨E1,E2⟩𝚒𝚗𝚕𝚎𝚝a=c⋅𝟷𝚒𝚗𝚕𝚎𝚝b=c⋅𝟸𝚒𝚗E3\mathtt{par}(E_{1};E_{2};a.b.E_{3})\triangleq\mathtt{let}\;c=\langle E_{1},E_{2}\rangle\;\mathtt{in}\;\mathtt{let}\;a=c\cdot\mathtt{1}\;\mathtt{in}\;\mathtt{let}\;b=c\cdot\mathtt{2}\;\mathtt{in}\;E_{3}

As before, there is the notion of evaluation:

  1. 1.

    M⇓cVM\Downarrow^{c}V when M↦cVM\mapsto^{c}V and V​𝗏𝖺𝗅V\;\mathsf{val}.

  2. 2.

    M⇓VM\Downarrow V when there is a cc s.t. M⇓cVM\Downarrow^{c}V.

However, cc now represents the span, i.e., the parallel complexity of the computation MM. The construction of the type system τω\tau_{\omega} and the associated proof theory is unaffected by the change of the operational semantics.

There is an associated derived binary sequencing rule:

To demonstrate the type theory when instrumented with the parallel operational semantics, we analyze the Fibonacci function when implemented directly as specified by the recursive definition:

F⁡(n)={0​ if ​n=01​ if ​n=1F⁡(n−1)+F⁡(n−2)​ o.w. F(n)=\begin{cases}0\text{ if }n=0\\ 1\text{ if }n=1\\ F(n-1)+F(n-2)\text{ o.w. }\end{cases}
